topic.title: Translating an Oxygen User Manual with Content Fusion
topic.shortdesc: How we used the AI translation agent in Content Fusion to translate the Content Fusion Cloud user manual into French, and what we learned about getting a translation that matches the product.

body.p: In The Translation Workflow for the AI Era, we introduced the AI translation workflow in Content Fusion. In this post, we show how we used it to translate a real manual, the Content Fusion Cloud user guide, into French.

The agent’s French is fluent from the first run. To make it match the product, we did two things: we gave it the product’s UI strings and approved terms, and we reviewed every result. The steps below show how.

image.alt: Each release goes through branch, prepare the translation resources (UI strings, terminology, and project rules, which guide every job), translate, review (a quick check, an AI review, and an expert review), and integrate and publish. Issues found by the reviews are fixed at their cause, and the affected topics are translated again.

ol.li: Create a translation branch: keep the translation work apart from the source content.
Prepare the translation resources: give the agent the product's UI strings, the approved terminology, and the project rules.
Translate: run a translation job and bring its results into your workspace.
Review the translation: check the result with a quick check, an AI review, and a bilingual expert, then fix each issue at its cause.
Integrate and publish: merge the translation branch and publish the translated manual.

body.p: Do all the translation work on a dedicated Git branch. The branch keeps the translated files apart from the source content. This matters during the review: the reviewer compares each translated topic with its English source, and the source must not change while they do it. When the translation is approved, you merge the branch back.

image.alt: A translation branch is created from the main branch, which holds the English source. The translation, the review, and the fixes are committed on that branch, which is then merged back into the main branch, tagged, and published.

body.p: In Content Fusion, create the branch from the one that holds the English content, and name it with a pattern such as translation/translate--<product-name>--<lang> (for example, translation/translate--Content-Fusion-Cloud--fr-FR). See Branch Management in the Oxygen Content Fusion User Guide.

Do this step for every release, on the translation branch. The first time, you create the resource files. After that, you update them: update the UI strings file from the new build, because labels change between releases, and add the terms of the new features to the terminology file.

When you translate technical documentation for a software product, two kinds of words need special care: terminology and UI strings. They look similar at first glance, and they often overlap, but they follow different rules.

Content Fusion does not have built-in support for these concepts, but it has a powerful mechanism that allows users to specify additional prompts at two levels: per job, which you can configure when creating a translation job, or per project, which applies to all translation jobs in that project. In our case, we'll use the per-project mechanism.

section.title: Where the agent finds the project rules
section.p: The agent reads the project rules from .contentfusion/i18n/agent-instructions.md and applies them to every translation job, on top of its built-in rules.

For the Oxygen user manuals, the project rules are split across three files in .contentfusion/i18n/. agent-instructions.md holds the general rules. The two large lists, the UI strings and the terminology, have their own file for each product and language. The agent loads only the lists that the current job needs:

row.entry: The rules for every translation, the list of products, and how to use the next two files.
The product's translated UI labels and messages.
The approved translation of each product concept, and the terms that stay in English.

section.p: In these paths, <product> is the product's resource folder (fusion for Content Fusion) and <lang> is the language tag. The UI strings file writes it with an underscore (fr_FR), and the terminology file with a hyphen (fr-FR).
All these files are public. You can find them in the .contentfusion/i18n folder of the Oxygen user guide repository on GitHub, and use them as a starting point for your own manuals.

section.title: UI strings and terminology: what is the difference?
section.p: Both files tell the agent which words to use, but in different ways:

ul.li: A UI string is copied exactly. The reader must find it on screen, so the agent never changes it. If the label does not fit the grammar of the sentence, the agent rewrites the sentence around the label.
A term is adapted to the sentence. It fixes which word to use for a concept, but the word can change its form: singular or plural, with or without an article, and so on.

section.p: In short, terminology is about saying the same thing the same way, while UI strings are about saying exactly what’s on the screen. Getting both right, and keeping them in sync with each other, is what makes a translated manual feel trustworthy.

section.title: UI strings
section.p: UI strings are the exact pieces of text that appear in the software’s interface, such as button labels, menu items, dialog titles, and messages. When a manual says “Click Save As,” the translated version must match the localized interface word for word, or the user won’t find what they’re looking for on the screen. UI strings come from the software’s own resource files, change with every release, and leave the translator no room to rephrase.
The UI strings file is a table generated from the product's own translation files. Each row gives a string's ID, its English text, its translation, and where it appears:
section.codeblock: | ID | Source (en-US) | Target (fr_FR) | Context | |---|---|---|---| | save | Save | Enregistrer | Save button label; Generic save button text | | activity | Task activity | Activité de tâche | Section title for the activity stream related to a task. |
section.p: The agent uses the Target text exactly as it is. These French examples show why:

row.entry: The Task activity section lists the comments.
La section Activité de la tâche affiche les commentaires.
La section Activité de tâche affiche les commentaires.

section.p: Each wrong translation reads well, but the reader cannot find the label on screen.

section.title: Terminology
section.p: Terminology is the vocabulary of your domain and product: the concepts your users need to understand, like “review task,” “workspace,” or “translation index.” The goal is consistency of meaning: the same concept should always be expressed the same way, even though the translated term can still adapt to the grammar of the sentence.

The terminology file holds the concepts of the product and its domain, such as repository, branch, or publication, and the names that must stay in English. It has two tables: Terms and Do not translate.
The Terms table gives the approved translation of each concept. The Details column adds the grammar the agent needs (part of speech, gender), the translations to avoid, and example sentences:
section.codeblock: | Source | Target | Context | Details | |---|---|---|---| | workspace | espace de travail | user's working copy of a project | pos: noun; gender: m; ex: from a card in your workspace → depuis une fiche de votre espace de travail | | review task | tâche de révision | unit of review work in Content Fusion | pos: noun; gender: f; deprecated: tâche d'examen; deprecated: tâche de revue |
section.p: The agent always uses the approved word, but adapts its form to the sentence:

row.entry: The review tasks are listed in your workspace.
Les tâches de révision sont listées dans votre espace de travail.
Fermez toutes les tâches de révision.

section.p: The Do not translate table lists the terms that stay in English: product and brand names, acronyms, file names, and code. The Note column tells the agent how the term behaves in the target language:
section.codeblock: | Term | Kind | Note | |---|---|---| | Content Fusion | product | short product name | | DITA map | name | feminine in French (la DITA map), plural DITA maps; map alone → carte |
section.p: For example, Open the DITA map. becomes Ouvrez la DITA map., not Ouvrez la carte DITA.

body.p: The agent translates only the files that need it. For each source file, it checks the translation index (.contentfusion/i18n/translation-index.xml) and finds one of three states:

ul.li: Missing: the file was never translated into this language. The agent translates it.

Stale: the English source changed after the last translation. The agent translates it again, and uses the existing translation as context, so the earlier wording and your manual corrections are kept where they still apply.
Current: the translation matches the English source. The agent skips it.

body.p: That is why you can run this step again at any time to update a translation.

ol.li: In Content Fusion, open the User Guide project, and check that the translation branch is selected in the top stripe.

Click New translation, and set these fields:
Publications: the publication of the manual to translate.
Target Languages: one or more target languages.
Translation Instructions: extra instructions for this job, in plain language. For example, tell the agent which product the manual describes and where to save the translated files.
Example:Translations are for product: `Content Fusion`.
Save translations to `DITA-cf/i18n/fusion-cloud/fr-FR/`, mirroring the source structure inside it.

section.title: The first translation into a language
section.p: The first job for a language also creates the translation index entries, the translated maps, a copy of every image, and the deliverables for the new language. It copies the deliverables that already exist for English. See The First Time You Translate a Project in the Oxygen Content Fusion User Guide.

section.title: Follow the job
section.p: The job appears as a card in your workspace. The card shows the current step and the progress. You can stop the job from the card.
section.note: While the job runs, do not change the source files or the translated files that it covers. Your changes can conflict with the files that the agent writes.
section.p: If the job fails, click View log on the card to see the cause. For example, the job fails when your organization runs out of AI credits. If the job produced some files before it failed, select Bring partial results into workspace to keep them. To run the same job again, select Re-run from the card's menu.
For more, see Managing a Translation Job in the Oxygen Content Fusion User Guide.

section.title: Bring the translation into your workspace

ol.li: When the job finishes, click Bring into workspace on the card. The translated files and the updated translation index are added to your workspace as uncommitted changes.

Commit the files to the translation branch.
A reviewer can open the translated files only after you commit them.

body.p: An AI translation reads fluently, and that is exactly what makes its mistakes easy to miss. A sentence can sound perfect and still name a button that does not exist on screen, translate the same concept in two different ways, or quietly drop a clause from the source. To catch them, you can review the translation with one of these methods, or combine several of them:

ul.li: A quick check: before you commit, you make sure that the job changed the right files and left valid DITA with no broken links.
An AI review: an AI agent reads every translated topic and flags wrong terms, UI labels that do not match the product, inconsistencies, and missing text.
An expert review: a bilingual reviewer judges what no rule can check: whether the translation means the same thing as the source, and whether it sounds natural.

section.title: Start with a quick check
section.p: This check takes only a few minutes, and it is worth doing every time: right after you bring the translation into your workspace, and before you commit it. Two views in Content Fusion tell you most of what you need to know:

ul.li: Changes view: lists every file that the job added or modified. Expect the translated topics, the translation index and, for a new language, the deliverables. If an English topic shows up in the list, something went wrong.
Problems view: shows the validation errors. The translated publication should be valid DITA, and the Problems view helps you make sure that your project stays valid when you commit your changes.

section.p: For details, see Reviewing Translations Before You Commit in the Oxygen Content Fusion User Guide.

section.title: Let an AI agent review every topic
section.p: A human reviewer rarely has the time to read every topic of a large manual. An AI agent does, and it never gets tired of comparing a translation with its source, sentence by sentence.

To guide the agent, we wrote a review prompt that you can download and adapt to your own manuals. It asks the agent to compare every translated topic with its English source and to look for six kinds of problems:

ul.li: Terminology: a term that does not use its approved translation.
UI terminology: a menu, button, or dialog name that does not match the product's UI strings.
Language quality: grammar, spelling, and the typography of the target language, such as the non-breaking space before a colon in French.
Accuracy and completeness: text that is missing, added, or that changes the meaning of the source.
Consistency: the same concept translated in different ways in different topics.
Style and naturalness: text that reads like a translation, not like a manual written in the target language.

section.p: You do not need a separate tool to run the review. Save the prompt in your repository (we keep it in translation/review-prompt.md), then run the review as a translation job that translates nothing. With the translation branch selected, start a new translation job for the translated publication and the language to review, and use the Translation Instructions field to point the agent to the prompt instead:
section.codeblock: Do not translate anything. Follow the instructions in `translation/review-prompt.md`, with TARGET_LANG = fr-FR.
section.p: Write the language tag exactly as it appears in the translation index. The agent finds the translated topics in the index, applies the same project rules as the translation agent, and writes its findings to translation-review-<lang>.md at the root of the repository. When the job finishes, bring it into your workspace and open the report.

You do not have to read the report from top to bottom. Start with the Root-cause rollup table at the top: a handful of root causes usually explain most of the issues, and the table tells you where to fix each one. Then go through the issue records. Each one shows the source text, the current translation, and a recommended translation.
The same approach works for any other question you have about your translation. See Asking the Agent a Question in the Oxygen Content Fusion User Guide.

section.title: Ask a bilingual expert
section.p: The AI review is good at checking rules: the approved term, the exact UI label, the French typography. A reviewer who knows both languages judges what no rule covers: whether the translation says the same thing as the source, and whether it reads like a manual that was written in French. The reviewer reads each translated topic side by side with its English source, in the tool that suits them best:

ul.li: Content Fusion: create a project review task on the translation branch, include the translated topics, and invite the reviewer. The reviewer edits the topics or adds comments in the browser, and you then integrate the accepted changes into the translation branch. See Creating a Project Review Task.
Oxygen XML Editor: the reviewer checks out the translation branch and works locally, with the source and the translation open side by side. This suits reviewers who prefer a desktop editor.

section.note: Attach the PDF of the English manual to the review task, so the reviewer sees each topic in its context.

section.title: Fix each issue at its cause
section.p: It is tempting to correct every issue directly in the translated topic. This is the right fix when the mistake appears only once. But if the agent made the mistake because of a missing term or an unclear rule, it will make the same mistake again in the next release. So, before you fix an issue, ask where it comes from:

row.entry: A one-off mistake in a single topic

Commit the change. Later jobs skip the topic while its English source is unchanged. When the source changes, the agent uses your corrected translation as context, so your wording is kept where it still applies.
A wrong or missing term or UI string, or a rule that the agent did not follow
The terminology file, the UI strings file, or agent-instructions.md
An error or unclear text in the English source
The English topic, on the translation branch
The topic becomes stale, so the next job translates it again. The fix reaches the source branch when you merge the translation branch.

section.note: Fix the English source only after the review is complete. This way, the reviewers always compare the translation with the source it was made from.

section.title: Retranslate after you change the rules
section.p: There is one catch. The agent decides what to translate by looking only at the English source: if a topic has not changed since its last translation, the next job skips it. A new term in the terminology file or a new rule in agent-instructions.md does not change any source, so it does not trigger a new translation by itself.
To force it, remove the topics from the translation index:

ol.li: In .contentfusion/i18n/translation-index.xml, delete the entries of the topics you want to translate again. These topics become missing.
Commit the change, then run the translation again.
Review the new translation of these topics.

section.note: The next job overwrites these topics. If you corrected some of them by hand, commit your corrections first, so you can restore them from the Git history.
section.p: Repeat this review and fix cycle until the review finds no more important issues, then continue with Step 5: Integrate and publish.

body.p: When the review is complete, merge the translation branch back into the branch you created it from. The merge brings the translated files, the updated translation index, and any source fixes from the review.

ol.li: In Content Fusion, select the target branch in the top stripe.
From the branch drop-down menu, select Merge into current branch..., then select the translation branch.
Optional: publish the translated manual from the project's Deliverables page. The first translation job created the deliverables for the new language.

body.p: For details, see Branch Management in the Oxygen Content Fusion User Guide.
body.note: Mark the release with a Git tag. A tag records the exact commit of each translation release, so you can later compare two releases, or rebuild the manual exactly as it was published.
